Reference: Faber and Gaubert (2019)

Model Setting

The paper studies the long-run economic consequences of tourism, a fast-growing services export of developing countries, both locally and in the aggregate. The conventional view holds that agglomeration economies reside in manufacturing, so that a reallocation of factors into services could act as a form of Dutch disease. The setting is Mexico, where tourism emerged in the 1950s and 1960s and now accounts for about 10 percent of GDP; the 150 coastal municipalities (14 percent of the population) receive 63.5 percent of national hotel revenues, and roughly 80 percent of tourism revenue comes from domestic visitors and 20 percent from foreigners. The paper proceeds in two parts. The first estimates the local effects of tourism in the cross-section of 2,455 municipalities, using geological, oceanographic and archaeological variation in ex ante tourism attractiveness along the coastline as instruments for local hotel revenues. The second builds a quantitative spatial equilibrium model in the spirit of Allen and Arkolakis (2014), Ahlfeldt et al. (2015) and Redding (2016), with trade in goods, trade in tourism services through travelling consumers, labour mobility, input-output linkages, tax-financed public investment in tourism, and within-sector and cross-sector agglomeration spillovers on manufacturing. Because cross-sectional regressions identify only relative effects, the model is needed to recover the aggregate implications that are consistent with the estimated local effects.

The main findings are as follows. A 10 percent increase in local hotel revenues raises municipality employment by 2.5 percent and nominal GDP by 4 percent, in part through a multiplier effect on manufacturing GDP of 3.9 percent. Through the lens of the model, about 60 percent of the local GDP effect comes from neoclassical forces and the rest from agglomeration forces, with an estimated within-manufacturing spillover elasticity of 0.064 and a cross-sector spillover elasticity of 0.087 from services to manufacturing. Tourism raises the welfare of the average Mexican household by 4.64 percent net of the cost of public investment, of which about 40 percent (1.82 percent) is due to international tourism. Spillovers contribute only about one-tenth of the aggregate gain (the gain would be 4.25 percent without them): they generate large reallocations towards touristic regions, but the local gains are largely offset by lower agglomeration economies in less touristic regions, so the national gains mainly reflect a classical market integration effect.

Reduced-Form Evidence and Instruments

The baseline specification for municipality nnn in coastal group ccc and census year ttt is:

log⁡(ynt)=αct+β TourismAttractivenessn+α′Xnt+ϵnt(6.4.8.1)\log\left(y_{nt}\right)=\alpha_{ct}+\beta\,TourismAttractiveness_n+\alpha'X_{nt}+\epsilon_{nt} \tag{6.4.8.1}log(ynt​)=αct​+βTourismAttractivenessn​+α′Xnt​+ϵnt​(6.4.8.1)

where ynty_{nt}ynt​ is an outcome (employment, population, wage bill, GDP by sector, Mincerized wages) in 2000 and 2010 for the population censuses or in 1998 and 2008 for the Censos Economicos, αct\alpha_{ct}αct​ are coast-by-period fixed effects, and XntX_{nt}Xnt​ are predetermined controls (log distance to Mexico City and to the US border, log area, dummies for state capitals, historical cities and colonial ports, log temperature and precipitation). The coefficient β\betaβ of this regression is distinct from the tourism parameter β\betaβ of the model below. Standard errors are clustered by municipality. Three measures of attractiveness are used: (i) a dummy for an offshore island within 5 km of the coastline; (ii) the fraction of pixels within 100 m of the shoreline covered by white sand beach, classified from 1987-1997 LandSat images at 30 m resolution as falling within the wavelength ranges of the eight top-ranked Mexican beaches; and (iii) a dummy for pre-Hispanic archaeological ruins. Since the island and beach measures are zero inland and the fixed effects are coast-by-period, the identifying variation is within coastal municipalities. Because tourism was negligible before 1960, the cross-section captures the long-run effect of tourism exposure.

In the reduced form, a one standard deviation increase in a standardized attractiveness score raises employment by 33 percent, population by 24 percent, the wage bill by about 80 percent, GDP by 74 percent, manufacturing GDP by about 45 percent (coefficient 0.451) and Mincerized wages by 7.6 percent. Placebo regressions on census populations of 1921-1950 give small, negative and insignificant coefficients; model-based residential amenities are not significantly correlated with the instruments; and a panel design that interacts attractiveness with national tourist arrivals (instrumented with US air fares) confirms the results. The IV specification replaces attractiveness by log hotel sales (inverse hyperbolic sine), instrumented with the three measures jointly (first-stage F-statistic 15.13). The IV coefficients, with standard errors in parentheses, are 0.245 (0.041) for employment, 0.200 (0.042) for population, 0.475 (0.069) for labour income, 0.404 (0.071) for GDP, 0.394 (0.094) for manufacturing GDP, 0.102 (0.150) for agricultural GDP and 0.0446 (0.0057) for the wage residual. Overidentification tests do not reject (p-values between 0.14 and 0.70). The manufacturing effect remains sizable in sectors with below-median tourism input intensity. The instruments also raise the stock of public investment in tourism (coefficients 2.05, 31.5 and 0.97 for the island, beach and ruins measures) and improve access to transport infrastructure, which motivates modelling public investment as an input to tourism; excluding or controlling for distance to government-planned tourism centres, which absorbed more than 90 percent of public spending on tourism, leaves the IV estimates essentially unchanged. A positive effect on manufacturing is not by itself evidence of productivity spillovers, since with trade costs, labour mobility and input-output linkages it could arise from neoclassical demand linkages alone.

With spillovers and input-output linkages uniqueness is not guaranteed: the sufficient conditions of Allen, Arkolakis and Li do not apply because tourism and manufacturing have different trade elasticities, workers are mobile and productivity is endogenous.

Welfare and Counterfactual Equilibria

Welfare is measured by the average utility of workers living in a region. With free mobility and Frechet shocks it is equalized across Mexican regions:

with K2=Γ(κ−1κ)LMϵK_2=\Gamma\left(\frac{\kappa-1}{\kappa}\right)L_{\mathcal{M}}^{\epsilon}K2​=Γ(κκ−1​)LMϵ​ and K3=Γ(κ−1κ)LM1/κK_3=\Gamma\left(\frac{\kappa-1}{\kappa}\right)L_{\mathcal{M}}^{1/\kappa}K3​=Γ(κκ−1​)LM1/κ​. Welfare is a power mean across regions of local utility, which consists of after-tax real income and amenities. The second line follows from substituting the labour supply equation into the first, which gives K3=K2LM1/κ~K_3=K_2L_{\mathcal{M}}^{1/\tilde{\kappa}}K3​=K2​LM1/κ~​ and, using 1/κ~=1/κ−ϵ1/\tilde{\kappa}=1/\kappa-\epsilon1/κ~=1/κ−ϵ, the constant stated here; the paper prints the Gamma term of K3K_3K3​ with exponent −1-1−1, which is inconsistent with its own K2K_2K2​ (the constants cancel in all comparisons). Since amenities BnB_nBn​ are fixed, the second line implies that the proportional welfare change between two equilibria can be read off any single region:

U^M=(1−ι)^(w^nP^MT,n)αMTL^n−1κ~,∀n∈M(6.4.8.21)\hat{U}_{\mathcal{M}}=\widehat{(1-\iota)}\left(\frac{\hat{w}_n}{\hat{P}_{MT,n}}\right)^{\alpha_{MT}}\hat{L}_n^{-\frac{1}{\tilde{\kappa}}},\qquad\forall n\in\mathcal{M} \tag{6.4.8.21}U^M​=(1−ι)​(P^MT,n​w^n​​)αMT​L^n−κ~1​​,∀n∈M(6.4.8.21)

where a hat denotes the ratio of the counterfactual to the baseline value. A region that gains in real income attracts population until the common welfare level is restored, so the welfare difference between two equilibria is identical across regions regardless of their exposure to tourism.

The gains from tourism are defined by comparing the observed equilibrium with a counterfactual in which the government provides no tourism capital, so that tourism productivity is zero everywhere in Mexico and both domestic and international tourism disappear, with all other fundamentals unchanged. No tax is levied in that counterfactual, so the measure is net of the cost of tourism infrastructure. The paper reports the inverse of the welfare loss from removing tourism. A second counterfactual imposes prohibitive frictions on international tourism only, keeping tourism between Mexican regions, and scales investment and the tax by the share of domestic tourism in total tourism in Mexico:

ι^=G^n=∑n∈MwnLn(1−χn)(∑i∈Mλni)∑n=1NwnLn(1−χn)(∑i∈Mλni)(6.4.8.22)\hat{\iota}=\hat{G}_n=\frac{\sum_{n\in\mathcal{M}}w_nL_n\left(1-\chi_n\right)\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}}\lambda_{ni}\right)}{\sum_{n=1}^Nw_nL_n\left(1-\chi_n\right)\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}}\lambda_{ni}\right)} \tag{6.4.8.22}ι^=G^n​=∑n=1N​wn​Ln​(1−χn​)(∑i∈M​λni​)∑n∈M​wn​Ln​(1−χn​)(∑i∈M​λni​)​(6.4.8.22)

Counterfactuals are solved with exact hat algebra (Dekle, Eaton and Kortum 2007; Caliendo et al. 2018; Redding 2016): the equilibrium conditions are written in changes relative to the baseline, so that a change in the tax (ι^=0\hat{\iota}=0ι^=0) or in travel frictions t^ni\hat{t}_{ni}t^ni​ can be evaluated given the parameters (νjj′,αMT,αG,β,θ,ρ,κ~)(\nu^{j'}_j,\alpha_{MT},\alpha_G,\beta,\theta,\rho,\tilde{\kappa})(νjj′​,αMT​,αG​,β,θ,ρ,κ~) and the baseline values of (πnj,λnj,χn,wn,LM,n,LT,n,LS,n,Gn)(\pi_{nj},\lambda_{nj},\chi_n,w_n,L_{M,n},L_{T,n},L_{S,n},G_n)(πnj​,λnj​,χn​,wn​,LM,n​,LT,n​,LS,n​,Gn​). The system in changes is in the online appendix and is not reproduced in the main text. Because uniqueness is not guaranteed, the algorithm selects the counterfactual equilibrium closest to the observed one: it starts from baseline values and iterates on a weighted average of the previous guess and the newly solved values until convergence.

Role of Local Spillovers

Let sM,ns_{M,n}sM,n​ be the share of workers of region nnn employed in manufacturing. The productivity equation can be rewritten as:

Mn=MnosM,nγM(1−sM,n)γSLnγS+γM(6.4.8.23)M_n=M^o_ns_{M,n}^{\gamma_M}\left(1-s_{M,n}\right)^{\gamma_S}L_n^{\gamma_S+\gamma_M} \tag{6.4.8.23}Mn​=Mno​sM,nγM​​(1−sM,n​)γS​LnγS​+γM​​(6.4.8.23)

The term LnγS+γML_n^{\gamma_S+\gamma_M}LnγS​+γM​​ is the agglomeration effect. Touristic regions attract workers, which raises their manufacturing productivity, but since total population is fixed and the elasticity is constant, gains in some regions are offset by losses in others, so the aggregate effect is muted, as in Kline and Moretti (2014). The term sM,nγM(1−sM,n)γSs_{M,n}^{\gamma_M}(1-s_{M,n})^{\gamma_S}sM,nγM​​(1−sM,n​)γS​ is the sectoral reallocation effect. It is maximized at an interior sectoral mix, sM,n=γM/(γM+γS)s_{M,n}=\gamma_M/(\gamma_M+\gamma_S)sM,n​=γM​/(γM​+γS​): an equal balance when γS=γM\gamma_S=\gamma_MγS​=γM​, and full specialization in manufacturing when γS=0\gamma_S=0γS​=0. Tourism lowers sM,ns_{M,n}sM,n​. In regions with a high initial manufacturing share this moves the local economy towards the optimal balance and reinforces the agglomeration effect; in regions with a low initial manufacturing share it moves the economy away from the balance and works against it. The aggregate productivity effect of tourism therefore depends on γM\gamma_MγM​, γS\gamma_SγS​ and on how initial sectoral shares covary with tourism attractiveness, and it can be positive or negative.

Calibration and Estimation

The model is calibrated to the mean of inflation-adjusted outcomes for 2000 and 2010. The 2,455 municipalities are aggregated to 300 regions (the 150 coastal municipalities, and 150 interior centres at the centroids of the largest interior municipalities), plus a Rest of the World aggregate. Wages wnw_nwn​ and employment LnL_nLn​ come from the population censuses. Input-output shares come from the 2003 Mexican input-output table, and αMT\alpha_{MT}αMT​ and αS\alpha_SαS​ are set so that aggregate value-added shares of traded and non-traded sectors match the national accounts. Regional manufacturing GDP is observed; regional tourism GDP is hotel sales scaled by a common factor so that the aggregate ratio of tourism to manufacturing GDP matches the national accounts; services employment is then implied by the model, which delivers (LS,n,LT,n,LM,n)(L_{S,n},L_{T,n},L_{M,n})(LS,n​,LT,n​,LM,n​). Public investment GnG_nGn​ is the municipality stock of tourism investment converted into steady-state annual flows; αG=0.036\alpha_G=0.036αG​=0.036 is the ratio of government investment to tourism GDP, and ι=0.5%\iota=0.5\%ι=0.5% is total annualized investment over GDP. Border frictions for goods and tourism are chosen to match aggregate flows between Mexico and the rest of the world, and frictions within Mexico are functions of the distance dnjd_{nj}dnj​ between regional centroids:

τnj−θ=dnj−DM,tnj−β=dnj−DT,(n,j)∈M×M(6.4.8.24)\tau_{nj}^{-\theta}=d_{nj}^{-D_M},\qquad t_{nj}^{-\beta}=d_{nj}^{-D_T},\qquad(n,j)\in\mathcal{M}\times\mathcal{M} \tag{6.4.8.24}τnj−θ​=dnj−DM​​,tnj−β​=dnj−DT​​,(n,j)∈M×M(6.4.8.24)

with DM=1D_M=1DM​=1 from the literature and DT=0.96D_T=0.96DT​=0.96 (standard error 0.043) estimated by Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood on bilateral tourism exports of 115 countries over 1990-2011 with origin-by-year and destination-by-year fixed effects and controls for common border, language, colonial ties and visa requirements. The goods trade elasticity is θ=6.1\theta=6.1θ=6.1 (Adao, Costinot and Donaldson 2017). The tourism elasticity is set at the upper bound supported by panel data on bilateral tourism flows and relative consumption prices, 1+β=2.51+\beta=2.51+β=2.5, and the upper-nest elasticity, which cannot exceed the lower-nest value, is set to ρ=2.5\rho=2.5ρ=2.5; both choices are conservative for the gains from tourism. The remaining estimation has three steps.

  • Step 1, regional fundamentals: given (wn,LM,n,LS,n,LT,n,Gn)(w_n,L_{M,n},L_{S,n},L_{T,n},G_n)(wn​,LM,n​,LS,n​,LT,n​,Gn​) and (νjj′,αMT,αG,β,θ,ρ)(\nu^{j'}_j,\alpha_{MT},\alpha_G,\beta,\theta,\rho)(νjj′​,αMT​,αG​,β,θ,ρ), the gravity equations, price indices and market-clearing conditions are inverted, following Redding (2016), to recover the unique shifters A~n\widetilde{A}_nAn​ and MnM_nMn​ (up to scale). With ZT,noZ^o_{T,n}ZT,no​ normalized to 1, A~n=AnGnβαG\widetilde{A}_n=A_nG_n^{\beta\alpha_G}An​=An​GnβαG​​ separates the fundamental component AnA_nAn​ from public investment. This step does not require κ~\tilde{\kappa}κ~, γM\gamma_MγM​ or γS\gamma_SγS​, and conditional on the data the inversion is unique even though counterfactual equilibria need not be.

  • Step 2, labour supply elasticity: the labour supply equation gives the regression shown below, in which the real wage is instrumented with the three attractiveness measures. The IV estimate is κ~=6.35\tilde{\kappa}=6.35κ~=6.35 against 1.91 by OLS, which is biased downward by labour demand variation and measurement error. The residuals, re-estimated excluding one instrument at a time, are the model-based amenities used in the robustness test.

  • Step 3, agglomeration elasticities: (γM,γS)(\gamma_M,\gamma_S)(γM​,γS​) are estimated by indirect inference from the six moment conditions shown below. The result is γ^M=0.064\hat{\gamma}_M=0.064γ^​M​=0.064 (bootstrap standard error 0.035) and γ^S=0.087\hat{\gamma}_S=0.087γ^​S​=0.087 (0.034).

The estimating equation of the second step is:

log⁡Ln=Ko+κ~log⁡((wnPMT,n)αMT)+ξnfor n∈M(6.4.8.25)\log L_n=K_o+\tilde{\kappa}\log\left(\left(\frac{w_n}{P_{MT,n}}\right)^{\alpha_{MT}}\right)+\xi_n\qquad\text{for }n\in\mathcal{M} \tag{6.4.8.25}logLn​=Ko​+κ~log((PMT,n​wn​​)αMT​)+ξn​for n∈M(6.4.8.25)

where KoK_oKo​ is a constant and ξn\xi_nξn​ contains log amenities. For the third step, the exclusion restrictions of the IV strategy imply that each instrument zn(j)z^{(j)}_nzn(j)​ (beach, island, ruins) is orthogonal to exogenous manufacturing productivity and to the population distribution LnoL^o_nLno​ that would prevail without tourism:

E[zn(j)log⁡Mno]=0,E[zn(j)log⁡Lno]=0,for j∈{1,2,3}(6.4.8.26)E\left[z^{(j)}_n\log M^o_n\right]=0,\qquad E\left[z^{(j)}_n\log L^o_n\right]=0,\qquad\text{for }j\in\{1,2,3\} \tag{6.4.8.26}E[zn(j)​logMno​]=0,E[zn(j)​logLno​]=0,for j∈{1,2,3}(6.4.8.26)

For each candidate pair (γM,γS)(\gamma_M,\gamma_S)(γM​,γS​) the no-tourism equilibrium is simulated from the otherwise fully calibrated model, the simulated log⁡Mno\log M^o_nlogMno​ and log⁡Lno\log L^o_nlogLno​ are regressed on each instrument conditional on the full set of controls, and the loss function is the sum of the six coefficients weighted by the inverse of their standard errors. The procedure thus finds the strength of spillovers needed to fit the observed correlation between regional outcomes and the instruments in today's equilibrium while imposing zero correlation in the no-tourism equilibrium, after accounting for input-output linkages, market access and migration. Both parameters are identified because the instruments move LST,nL_{ST,n}LST,n​ directly through tourism and LM,nL_{M,n}LM,n​ through spillovers and general equilibrium effects, and because population is a nonlinear function of all fundamentals, so the two sets of moments carry distinct information; the loss function is bowl-shaped with a single minimum. Standard errors and confidence intervals come from a bootstrap that treats wages, population, hotel sales and manufacturing GDP as noisy (a signal-to-noise ratio of 80 to 20) and accounts for sampling error in the parameters. A violation of the exclusion restriction that biases the local effects upward would bias both κ~\tilde{\kappa}κ~ and γS\gamma_SγS​ upward.

Quantitative Results

To link local and aggregate effects, the model-generated regional changes in GDP between the no-tourism equilibrium and today's equilibrium are regressed on today's tourism GDP, for each parameterization jjj of the agglomeration forces:

Δlog⁡GDP~nj=αcoastj+β1jlog⁡GDPTourismn+βj′Xn+ϵnj(6.4.8.27)\widetilde{\Delta\log GDP}^j_n=\alpha^j_{coast}+\beta^j_1\log GDPTourism_n+\beta^{j\prime}X_n+\epsilon^j_n \tag{6.4.8.27}ΔlogGDP​nj​=αcoastj​+β1j​logGDPTourismn​+βj′Xn​+ϵnj​(6.4.8.27)

with tourism GDP instrumented by the three measures as in the empirical section (300 regions, standard errors clustered by state).

  • Gains from tourism: the per capita welfare gain is 4.64 percent (95 percent confidence interval 3.01 to 9.03). International tourism accounts for 1.82 percent (0.80 to 5.09) and tourism between Mexican regions for the remainder. Without spillovers (γS=γM=0\gamma_S=\gamma_M=0γS​=γM​=0) the total gain would be 4.25 percent (3.20 to 6.85) and the international gain 2.38 percent (1.91 to 3.32).

  • No spillovers: the coefficient β1j\beta^j_1β1j​ is 0.232 (0.055), about 60 percent of the 0.4 estimated in the data. The effect on local manufacturing is negative: tourism raises local factor prices, and the gain in local market access from tourist and input demand is not enough to offset this.

  • Within-sector spillovers only (γM=0.15\gamma_M=0.15γM​=0.15, γS=0\gamma_S=0γS​=0): the coefficient falls to 0.048 (0.012), because the adverse effect on manufacturing is amplified by the loss of scale. According to the text the welfare gain falls to 0.47 percent, the Dutch disease case.

  • Cross-sector spillovers only (γS=0.15\gamma_S=0.15γS​=0.15, γM=0\gamma_M=0γM​=0): the coefficient is 0.657 (0.144), overshooting the data, and the aggregate gain is larger because manufacturing productivity grows. The last row of the paper's table lists 6.85 percent under the within-sector column and 0.47 percent under this column, the reverse of what the text describes; the text is the economically coherent reading (6.85 percent here).

  • Estimated parameters: the coefficient is 0.409 (0.090), almost identical to the empirical estimate of 0.404. The reduced-form coefficients are 0.561 (island), 10.02 (beach) and 0.021 (ruins).

  • Local versus aggregate: the two spillovers reinforce each other locally and explain about 40 percent of the local GDP effect, but add only about 10 percent to aggregate welfare, because productivity gains in touristic regions are offset by losses in regions that lose employment.

  • International tourism: spillovers reduce the gain (1.82 against 2.38 percent). The regions most exposed to international tourism have lower initial manufacturing shares than those exposed to domestic tourism, so reallocation towards services moves them further from the optimal sectoral mix, and the loss of manufacturing scale dominates the gain in services scale.

  • Robustness: for κ~\tilde{\kappa}κ~ between 2.35 and 6.35 and γS\gamma_SγS​ between 0 and 0.087 the gains range from 2.23 to 6.85 percent; a higher κ~\tilde{\kappa}κ~ lowers the gains and a higher γS\gamma_SγS​ raises them, so the two biases from a violated exclusion restriction work in opposite directions. Removing the part of tourism demand due to non-homothetic preferences gives 4.55 percent. Allowing tourism to reduce trade costs endogenously (three scenarios, including 50 percent reductions for tourism centres) leaves γS\gamma_SγS​ between 0.08 and 0.086 and gives gains of 4.61 to 5.23 percent.

This is the reduced-form estimating equation of the empirical part; nothing is derived from the model. The unit is municipality nnn in census year ttt, and ccc indexes the coastal versus non-coastal group. The outcome ynty_{nt}ynt​ is in logs, so the coefficient β\betaβ is a semi-elasticity: a one-unit increase in the attractiveness measure changes the outcome by approximately 100β100\beta100β percent. This β\betaβ is a regression coefficient and is unrelated to the Frechet shape parameter β\betaβ of equations (5), (6), (9) and (10).

The fixed effect αct\alpha_{ct}αct​ absorbs everything common to coastal (or inland) municipalities in a given period. Because the island and beach measures are zero inland, the coefficient is identified from comparisons among coastal municipalities in the same period, conditional on the predetermined controls XntX_{nt}Xnt​. The measure TourismAttractivenessnTourismAttractiveness_nTourismAttractivenessn​ has no time subscript: it is a fixed geological or archaeological feature, so the variation is purely cross-sectional and the coefficient captures a long-run effect of exposure to tourism.

In the IV version the regressor is replaced by log hotel sales and the three measures become excluded instruments,

log⁡(ynt)=αct+βlog⁡HotelSalesnt+α′Xnt+ϵnt,\log\left(y_{nt}\right)=\alpha_{ct}+\beta\log HotelSales_{nt}+\alpha'X_{nt}+\epsilon_{nt},log(ynt​)=αct​+βlogHotelSalesnt​+α′Xnt​+ϵnt​,

and identification requires that islands, white sand and ruins affect local outcomes only through tourism. The same instruments reappear in the model: in the labour supply regression (25), in the moment conditions (26) and in the model-based regression (27). The specification identifies only relative effects across municipalities; aggregate effects are absorbed by αct\alpha_{ct}αct​, which is why the structural model is needed.

This is the assumed utility function of a worker ω\omegaω who lives in region nnn; it is a primitive. It is multiplicative in four terms. CnC_nCn​ is the consumption aggregate of equation (3); because preferences are homothetic, CnC_nCn​ equals after-tax income divided by the consumer price index. BnB_nBn​ is an exogenous amenity of region nnn common to all residents. LnϵL_n^{\epsilon}Lnϵ​ makes the amenity endogenous to local population: ϵ<0\epsilon<0ϵ<0 is congestion, ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0 an amenity agglomeration force. εn(ω)\varepsilon_n(\omega)εn​(ω) is an idiosyncratic taste for living in nnn, independent across workers and regions, drawn from a Frechet distribution with shape κ\kappaκ.

The multiplicative Frechet form is chosen because the maximum of independent Frechet variables with a common shape is again Frechet. This yields closed forms for the location shares, equation (15), and for expected utility, equation (20). The shape κ\kappaκ governs how homogeneous tastes are: a large κ\kappaκ means little dispersion, so that small differences in CnBnLnϵC_nB_nL_n^{\epsilon}Cn​Bn​Lnϵ​ move many workers. In the limit of infinite κ\kappaκ the common component of utility is equalized across regions; for finite κ\kappaκ regional labour supply is upward sloping.

Only the combination

κ~=κ1−κϵ\tilde{\kappa}=\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa\epsilon}κ~=1−κϵκ​

is identified and used, as shown in the derivation of equation (15). It requires κϵ<1\kappa\epsilon<1κϵ<1, and κ>1\kappa>1κ>1 is needed for expected utility to be finite. The note states that the draw has mean 1; this normalization matters only for the constants K2K_2K2​ and K3K_3K3​ of equation (20), as discussed there.

This is the assumed consumption aggregator, a primitive. The outer nest is Cobb-Douglas between a traded bundle (weight αMT\alpha_{MT}αMT​) and local non-traded services CS,nC_{S,n}CS,n​ (weight αS=1−αMT\alpha_S=1-\alpha_{MT}αS​=1−αMT​). This is the assumed agglomeration technology, the central new element of the model; it is a primitive. Manufacturing productivity MnM_nMn​ is the product of an exogenous component MnoM^o_nMno​ (geography, natural advantage) and two external scale effects that individual firms take as given. LM,nγML_{M,n}^{\gamma_M}LM,nγM​​ is the within-sector spillover: productivity rises with local manufacturing employment with elasticity γM\gamma_MγM​, the standard localization economy. LST,nγSL_{ST,n}^{\gamma_S}LST,nγS​​ is the cross-sector spillover: productivity rises with local employment in services, LST,n=LT,n+LS,nL_{ST,n}=L_{T,n}+L_{S,n}LST,n​=LT,n​+LS,n​, with elasticity γS\gamma_SγS​. In logs,

log⁡Mn=log⁡Mno+γMlog⁡LM,n+γSlog⁡LST,n.\log M_n=\log M^o_n+\gamma_M\log L_{M,n}+\gamma_S\log L_{ST,n}.logMn​=logMno​+γM​logLM,n​+γS​logLST,n​.

The two elasticities decide whether tourism helps or hurts manufacturing beyond demand linkages. Tourism raises LST,nL_{ST,n}LST,n​ and, by bidding up local wages, tends to lower LM,nL_{M,n}LM,n​. With γM>0\gamma_M>0γM​>0 and γS=0\gamma_S=0γS​=0 this lowers productivity, the Dutch disease case. With γS>0\gamma_S>0γS​>0 a larger local services sector raises productivity, a reduced form for better business services, looser credit constraints, training and business networks.

Because spillovers are external, firms still face constant returns, so the Eaton-Kortum structure of equations (12) and (13) is unchanged, with MnθM_n^{\theta}Mnθ​ in the place of the technology parameter. The constant-elasticity form is what makes aggregate gains small: gains in regions that grow are offset by losses in regions that shrink, as equation (23) makes explicit. The elasticities are estimated from the moment conditions (26), giving γM=0.064\gamma_M=0.064γM​=0.064 and γS=0.087\gamma_S=0.087γS​=0.087. For instance, a 10 percent rise in local services employment at fixed manufacturing employment raises manufacturing productivity by about 0.087×log⁡(1.1)≈0.80.087\times\log(1.1)\approx0.80.087×log(1.1)≈0.8 percent.

This is the budget constraint of the Mexican government, an equilibrium condition rather than a derived result. The left-hand side is total spending on tourism capital, summed over Mexican regions; by equation (16) this spending is on the local manufacturing composite, so GnG_nGn​ is measured in units of expenditure. The right-hand side is the revenue of a proportional income tax at rate ι\iotaι on the wage bill wnLnw_nL_nwn​Ln​ of every Mexican region. There is no debt and no other spending, since the model is static.

The tax is national while spending is local: workers everywhere in Mexico pay the same rate, but GnG_nGn​ is concentrated in a few regions. This is why the tax term drops out of the location choice in equation (15) but lowers welfare for everybody in equation (20) through the factor 1−ι1-\iota1−ι. The allocation of GnG_nGn​ across regions is taken from the data and is not optimized.

Start from the productivity equation (14). The last factor is the agglomeration effect of total local scale, with elasticity γS+γM\gamma_S+\gamma_MγS​+γM​. To find the composition that maximizes it, take logs and differentiate with respect to sM,ns_{M,n}sM,n​:

ddsM,n[γMlog⁡sM,n+γSlog⁡(1−sM,n)]=γMsM,n−γS1−sM,n=0⟹sM,n=γMγM+γS.\frac{d}{ds_{M,n}}\left[\gamma_M\log s_{M,n}+\gamma_S\log\left(1-s_{M,n}\right)\right]=\frac{\gamma_M}{s_{M,n}}-\frac{\gamma_S}{1-s_{M,n}}=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad s_{M,n}=\frac{\gamma_M}{\gamma_M+\gamma_S}.dsM,n​d​[γM​logsM,n​+γS​log(1−sM,n​)]=sM,n​γM​​−1−sM,n​γS​​=0⟹sM,n​=γM​+γS​γM​​.

The log of the composition term is concave in sM,ns_{M,n}sM,n​, so this is a maximum. With equal elasticities the optimum is one half, and with γS=0\gamma_S=0γS​=0 it is full specialization in manufacturing. With the estimates γM=0.064\gamma_M=0.064γM​=0.064 and γS=0.087\gamma_S=0.087γS​=0.087 the productivity-maximizing manufacturing share is 0.064/0.151≈0.420.064/0.151\approx0.420.064/0.151≈0.42.

Tourism lowers sM,ns_{M,n}sM,n​ and raises LnL_nLn​ in touristic regions. The composition term rises if the region starts above the optimal share and falls if it starts below, so its sign varies across regions. For the scale term, total Mexican population is fixed, so inflows into touristic regions are outflows elsewhere, and with a constant elasticity the gains and losses largely offset in the aggregate. This decomposition is why the spillovers explain a large part of the local effects but only a small part of the aggregate welfare gain.

This is a parameterization of the unobserved bilateral frictions between Mexican regions; it is an assumption, not a result. Both the goods trade cost τnj\tau_{nj}τnj​ and the tourism travel cost tnjt_{nj}tnj​ are power functions of the distance dnjd_{nj}dnj​ between regional centroids. The frictions enter the model only through τnj−θ\tau_{nj}^{-\theta}τnj−θ​ in the goods gravity equation (12) and through tnj−βt_{nj}^{-\beta}tnj−β​ in the tourism gravity equation (9), so it is these composites that are parameterized. DMD_MDM​ and DTD_TDT​ are the distance elasticities of goods trade flows and of tourism flows. The implied elasticities of the frictions themselves are

τnj=dnjDM/θ,tnj=dnjDT/β,\tau_{nj}=d_{nj}^{D_M/\theta},\qquad t_{nj}=d_{nj}^{D_T/\beta},τnj​=dnjDM​/θ​,tnj​=dnjDT​/β​,

that is 1/6.1≈0.161/6.1\approx0.161/6.1≈0.16 for goods and 0.96/1.5=0.640.96/1.5=0.640.96/1.5=0.64 for tourism at the calibrated values.

The formulation is convenient because the model can be calibrated and solved without taking a separate stand on the level of trade costs: the shares in equations (9) and (12) depend on distance only through dnj−DTd_{nj}^{-D_T}dnj−DT​​ and dnj−DMd_{nj}^{-D_M}dnj−DM​​. For example, doubling the distance multiplies the bilateral term in tourism gravity by 2−0.96≈0.512^{-0.96}\approx0.512−0.96≈0.51 and that in goods gravity by 2−1=0.52^{-1}=0.52−1=0.5, holding origin and destination terms fixed.

DM=1D_M=1DM​=1 is the standard distance elasticity of trade. DT=0.96D_T=0.96DT​=0.96 is estimated from a gravity regression on bilateral tourism exports between countries with origin-by-year and destination-by-year fixed effects, which absorb the shifters and multilateral terms of equation (9), so that DTD_TDT​ is identified from bilateral variation in distance. The equation applies only to pairs of Mexican regions; frictions between Mexico and the rest of the world are set to match aggregate flows.

The estimating equation is the log of the labour supply equation (15). Taking logs:

log⁡Ln=log⁡LM−log⁡[∑k∈M(Bk(wkPMT,k)αMT)κ~]+κ~log⁡Bn+κ~log⁡((wnPMT,n)αMT).\log L_n=\log L_{\mathcal{M}}-\log\left[\sum_{k\in\mathcal{M}}\left(B_k\left(\frac{w_k}{P_{MT,k}}\right)^{\alpha_{MT}}\right)^{\tilde{\kappa}}\right]+\tilde{\kappa}\log B_n+\tilde{\kappa}\log\left(\left(\frac{w_n}{P_{MT,n}}\right)^{\alpha_{MT}}\right).logLn​=logLM​−log[k∈M∑​(Bk​(PMT,k​wk​​)αMT​)κ~]+κ~logBn​+κ~log((PMT,n​wn​​)αMT​).

The first two terms do not vary across regions. Let log⁡B‾\overline{\log B}logB​ be the mean of log amenities across Mexican regions and define

Ko≡log⁡LM−log⁡[∑k∈M(Bk(wkPMT,k)αMT)κ~]+κ~ log⁡B‾,ξn≡κ~(log⁡Bn−log⁡B‾).K_o\equiv\log L_{\mathcal{M}}-\log\left[\sum_{k\in\mathcal{M}}\left(B_k\left(\frac{w_k}{P_{MT,k}}\right)^{\alpha_{MT}}\right)^{\tilde{\kappa}}\right]+\tilde{\kappa}\,\overline{\log B},\qquad\xi_n\equiv\tilde{\kappa}\left(\log B_n-\overline{\log B}\right).Ko​≡logLM​−log[k∈M∑​(Bk​(PMT,k​wk​​)αMT​)κ~]+κ~logB​,ξn​≡κ~(logBn​−logB​).

Then

log⁡Ln=Ko+κ~log⁡((wnPMT,n)αMT)+ξn.\log L_n=K_o+\tilde{\kappa}\log\left(\left(\frac{w_n}{P_{MT,n}}\right)^{\alpha_{MT}}\right)+\xi_n.logLn​=Ko​+κ~log((PMT,n​wn​​)αMT​)+ξn​.

The slope is the spatial labour supply elasticity and the residual is the log amenity scaled by κ~\tilde{\kappa}κ~. By equation (20), KoK_oKo​ is a decreasing function of the common welfare level.

The regressor is constructed, not observed: wnw_nwn​ comes from the census and PMT,nP_{MT,n}PMT,n​ from the model inversion of the first calibration step. OLS is inconsistent. Amenities attract workers, which changes wages and prices, so ξn\xi_nξn​ is correlated with the real wage; the equation is a supply curve and one needs shifts in labour demand to trace it out; and measurement error in real wages attenuates the slope. The three attractiveness measures are used as instruments: they shift local labour demand through tourism, and the exclusion restriction is that they are uncorrelated with residential amenities BnB_nBn​. This is a strong assumption, since beaches could be valued directly by residents; the paper supports it with placebo tests. The IV estimate is 6.35 against 1.91 by OLS.

These are the six moment conditions that identify the spillover elasticities (γM,γS)(\gamma_M,\gamma_S)(γM​,γS​); they are identifying assumptions, not results. The index jjj here denotes one of the three instruments (beach, island, ruins), not a sector, and the expectation is across Mexican regions, conditional on the controls of equation (1). MnoM^o_nMno​ is the exogenous component of manufacturing productivity in equation (14), and LnoL^o_nLno​ is the population that region nnn would have in the equilibrium without tourism.

The assumption is that tourism attractiveness affects the economy only through tourism. Then it should be unrelated to a region's fundamental manufacturing productivity, and in a world without tourism it should not predict where people live. Neither MnoM^o_nMno​ nor LnoL^o_nLno​ is observed; both are computed from the model as functions of the parameters. For a candidate pair, invert equation (14),

log⁡Mno=log⁡Mn−γMlog⁡LM,n−γSlog⁡LST,n,\log M^o_n=\log M_n-\gamma_M\log L_{M,n}-\gamma_S\log L_{ST,n},logMno​=logMn​−γM​logLM,n​−γS​logLST,n​,

where MnM_nMn​ is recovered in the first calibration step independently of the elasticities; then simulate the no-tourism equilibrium to obtain LnoL^o_nLno​. The estimator chooses the pair that brings the six sample covariances closest to zero.

The intuition for identification is that in the data the instruments are positively correlated with LST,nL_{ST,n}LST,n​, LM,nL_{M,n}LM,n​ and MnM_nMn​. If the spillovers are set too low, the higher measured productivity of touristic regions is attributed to MnoM^o_nMno​ and the first moments are violated; if too high, the implied MnoM^o_nMno​ is negatively correlated with the instruments. The population moments add information because LnoL^o_nLno​ depends nonlinearly on all fundamentals. There are six moments for two parameters, so the model is overidentified. The same threat applies as in equation (25): a direct effect of beaches on productivity or amenities would bias the estimates.

This regression is run on model-generated data and connects the structural model back to the reduced-form evidence of equation (1). The dependent variable is the change in log GDP of region nnn between the simulated no-tourism equilibrium and today's equilibrium under parameterization jjj of the spillovers; here jjj indexes scenarios (no spillovers, within-sector only, cross-sector only, estimated values), not sectors. The regressor is today's log tourism GDP of the region, αcoastj\alpha^j_{coast}αcoastj​ is a coast fixed effect and XnX_nXn​ are the same controls as in the empirical section. Tourism GDP is instrumented with the three attractiveness measures, exactly as hotel sales are in the IV version of equation (1).

The coefficient β1j\beta^j_1β1j​ is the model counterpart of the empirical IV coefficient of 0.404 on log GDP. In the data the regression uses levels of log GDP, while here it uses the change from the no-tourism equilibrium; the two are comparable under the moment conditions (26), which say that the no-tourism outcomes are uncorrelated with the instruments:

Cov⁡(zn,log⁡GDPn)=Cov⁡(zn,Δlog⁡GDP~n)+Cov⁡(zn,log⁡GDPno),\operatorname{Cov}\left(z_n,\log GDP_n\right)=\operatorname{Cov}\left(z_n,\widetilde{\Delta\log GDP}_n\right)+\operatorname{Cov}\left(z_n,\log GDP^o_n\right),Cov(zn​,logGDPn​)=Cov(zn​,ΔlogGDP​n​)+Cov(zn​,logGDPno​),

where the last term is zero under the exclusion restriction.

The exercise serves two purposes. It is a validation: with the estimated spillovers the model gives 0.409, close to the data, although the estimation targets the moments in (26) and not this coefficient. And it is a decomposition: without spillovers the coefficient is 0.232, so neoclassical forces account for about 60 percent of the local effect and agglomeration forces for the rest. Comparing these local coefficients with the aggregate welfare numbers shows that large local effects need not translate into large aggregate gains.
